record.title: EvoHarnessBench reports competence losses as agent tool, skill and specialist pools expand
record.summary: The v3 preprint introduces EvoHarnessBench, which tests how agent performance changes as the externally supplied pool of tools, reusable skills or specialist agents expands. Its 17 constructed streams contain 802 unique tasks derived from two verifier-based agent benchmarks. The authors report that harness expansion alone can reduce performance on previously solved tasks, with reported declines varying across the tool, skill and agent tracks; adaptation gains are also inconsistent and retention can conflict with learning new capabilities. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent or production measurements.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The v3 preprint describes EvoHarnessBench, a controlled benchmark of externally expanding tool, skill, and specialist-agent harnesses, built from 17 multi-stage streams and 802 unique tasks drawn from verifier-based benchmarks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that exposing agents to cumulative expanding harnesses can lower performance on previously solved tasks even when the model and prompt stay fixed; the reported drops differ by tools, skills and specialist agents (12.1%, 13.8% and 46.4%, respectively).

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the paper's tested self-evolving methods and benchmark settings, gains are inconsistent, and retaining earlier competence can conflict with adapting to newly introduced capabilities.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper links benchmark materials, but the benchmark repository, task data, harness implementations and run configuration were not inspected in this review.
The reported harness-expansion effects and adaptation comparisons have not been independently reproduced.
The paper evaluates constructed streams from two verifier-based benchmark sources; real production harness growth and broader task distributions are not measured.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported effect generalizes, adding tools, reusable skills or specialist agents can reduce previously available agent competence and alter how systems should be evaluated and deployed. The result is important across agent research, but its evidence remains a paper-reported benchmark built from two task sources, so it does not establish production-scale impact.
limitations: All performance figures are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
The deployment evaluation holds model and prompt fixed while expanding the exposed harness; it does not establish that every real system will regress as tools or agents are added.
The 17 streams and 802 unique tasks are constructed from EnterpriseOps-Gym and Agents' Last Exam; they are not a representative sample of production workloads.
Skill-to-task association uses heuristic matching between skill content and verifier-checked outcomes, which the authors state may not identify necessary or sufficient skills.
Some tables compare system configurations with distinct underlying harnesses; the authors omit Claude Code from the main controlled comparison and report it separately.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
brief.summary: The v3 preprint introduces EvoHarnessBench, which tests how agent performance changes as the externally supplied pool of tools, reusable skills or specialist agents expands. Its 17 constructed streams contain 802 unique tasks derived from two verifier-based agent benchmarks. The authors report that harness expansion alone can reduce performance on previously solved tasks, with reported declines varying across the tool, skill and agent tracks; adaptation gains are also inconsistent and retention can conflict with learning new capabilities. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent or production measurements.

technical.claimed_result: In the deployment setting, the paper reports harness-induced performance drops of 12.1% for expanding tools, 13.8% for skills and 46.4% for specialist agents. The paper also reports inconsistent self-evolving adaptation across stages and environments. These measurements are author-reported.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports operating time and token metrics for benchmark runs, but this review did not normalize them into comparable monetary or energy costs.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v3 preprint specifies a benchmark with 17 multi-stage streams and 802 unique tasks instantiated across 1,510 axis-specific examples, 520 tools, 42 reference skills and 62 specialist agents. the research desk did not inspect or execute the linked benchmark artifact.
technical.implementation_status: A project page is linked from the arXiv HTML; the benchmark repository and its runnable artifacts were not inspected in this activation.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark derives cumulative harness stages from verifier-based tasks, progressively exposing additional tools, skills or specialist agents while retaining previously available capabilities. A deployment evaluation isolates the effect of broader exposure; a separate self-evolving setting tests persistent adaptation across stages.
technical.novelty: The study makes externally supplied harness growth itself a controlled source of non-stationarity, separate from changing task streams or capabilities learned by the agent.
technical.regime: The paper constructs 17 streams with three to six stages from EnterpriseOps-Gym and Agents' Last Exam. Controlled tool/skill comparisons use GPT-5-based systems; other multi-agent and adaptation configurations are reported by axis. Skill matching is heuristic. Claude Code is reported separately because it has a different underlying model and harness.
technical.reproducibility: The arXiv v3 HTML gives construction and evaluation details and links a project page, but artifacts were not audited and no independent run was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The task-specific harness reference exposes only capabilities annotated as required for each task, compared with the full cumulative harness in deployment evaluation. This is a controlled benchmark reference, not a production baseline.

brief.title: EvoHarnessBench reports competence losses as agent tool, skill and specialist pools expand
brief.why_it_matters: Agent systems increasingly gain tools, reusable procedures and specialist agents over time. This paper tests that growth as an evaluation variable and reports that broader harnesses can impair performance on earlier tasks, even when the underlying model and prompt remain fixed. The result motivates tracking retention separately from adaptation, while remaining limited to author-run benchmark streams rather than measured production systems.
